newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy govt calls confidence vote--more expected.
newsitem.headline: Italy govt calls confidence vote--more expected.

text.p: The Italian government on Tuesday called a fresh vote of confidence, its second within a week, to try to force a contested decree covering development projects through a recalcitrant parliament.

Environment Minister Edo Ronchi announced the new motion in the Chamber of Deputies (lower house) after a cabinet meeting. The vote was set for Wednesday and politicians expected more to be called soon.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government faces a legislation nightmare following a recent Constitutional Court ruling banning cabinets from the now traditional practice of re-issuing expiring draft government laws.
Measures passed by cabinet decree must now be turned into law by parliament within 60 days or dropped.
Opposition parties have seized on the decision to submerge decrees in amendments, forcing Prodi into life-or-death confidence votes to get the bills into law.
Massimo D'Alema, leader of the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), said the obstructionism was throwing parliament into convulsions.
"We have reached the very limits of the grotesque," he told reporters.
Prodi does not enjoy an absolute majority in the lower house of parliament and has to rely for support on the hard-left Communist Refoundation party.
Last week the government held a confidence vote on a decree covering a rescue plan for ailing bank Banco di Napoli.

Now it is moving to save a cabinet bill, due to expire on November 20, which will release funds for the development of rundown industrial areas in the northern city of Milan and the Bagnoli region of the southern port city of Naples.
The main thrust of the decree covers the Bagnoli project, which aims to turn a former steel works into a huge park surrounded by hotels, restaurants, beaches, a tourist marina and quality housing.
The federalist Northern League party has said further state aid for the development of the poorer south could not be justified and has snarled debate on the bill for months.

The main opposition bloc, the centre-right Freedom Alliance, headed by former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi, is supporting the League with its filibustering tactics, which affect far more than just the Bagnoli decree.

Political sources said on Thursday that opposition parties had presented over 6,000 amendments to a government bill setting up a watchdog body for the telecom sector, while thousands of amendments are expected to rain down on the government's 1997 budget when it goes before the lower house on Thursday.
Berlusconi said on Thursday he believed the government was preparing three or four confidence motions on the budget alone.
